Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verse 1:

(p-662) Surat "Al-'Alaq" (The Clot)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Mujahid: "It is the first surah that was revealed." However, the majority (al-Jumhur) hold that al-Fatiha was the first to be revealed, followed by Surat "Al-Qalam" (The Pen).

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. The place (mahall) of "bismi rabbika" is in the accusative (al-nasb), as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Read while beginning with the name of your Lord." It is as if it were said: "Say: In the name of Allah, then read." "Alladhi khalaq" (who created): no object is mentioned for "khalaqa," because the meaning is: "the One from whom creation proceeded and who alone possesses it, with no creator other than Him." Or its implied object is "kulla shay'" (everything), so that it encompasses every created thing, since it is unrestricted; thus some created things are not more deserving of His creating than others.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verse 2:

And His saying: ﴿Created man﴾ is a specification of man for mention, out of all that the word "creation" encompasses, because of his nobility, and because the revelation is directed to him. It is also permissible that what is meant is: "the One who created man," but He mentioned it in an ambiguous form and then explained it, as a magnification of His creation and as an indication of the wondrous nature of his innate disposition (fitrah).

﴿from a clinging clot﴾. And He used the plural, and did not say "from a clot" ('alaqah), because "al-insan" (man) carries the meaning of a collective (jam').

(p. 663) ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾, the One who has perfection in the increase of His generosity over every generous one, who bestows blessings upon His servants and shows forbearance toward them, so He does not hasten to punish them despite their disbelief and their denial of His blessings. It is as if there is no generosity beyond bestowing beneficial knowledge as a form of generosity, since He said:

Al-Nasafi's commentary on Surah 96, verse 4:

﴿Who taught﴾, writing,

﴿by the pen﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verse 5:

﴿He taught man that which he knew not﴾. Thereby He indicates the perfection of His generosity, in that He taught His servants what they did not know, and brought them forth from the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. He also draws attention to the virtue of the knowledge of writing (kitaba), because of the great benefits it contains. The sciences would not have been recorded (dawwanat), the wisdoms would not have been bound down (qayyadat), the reports of earlier peoples would not have been preserved (dabitat), nor would the revealed Books of God, except through writing. Were it not for it, the affairs of the religion and of the world would not have been set right. And even if there were no proof of the subtle wisdom of God except the matter of the pen (qalam) and the script (khatt), it would have been sufficient.

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Surah 96, verse 6:

﴿Nay (kalla)﴾: a rebuke (ra'd) directed at whoever disbelieves in the blessing of Allah upon him, by his transgression (tughyan), even though it is not mentioned, because the context indicates it.

﴿Indeed, man does transgress (layatgha)﴾: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, to the end of the surah.

"﴿That he saw himself﴾": that he saw (رَآهُ) himself, meaning أنْ رَأى نَفْسَهُ. It is said regarding the verbs of the heart: "رَأيْتُنِي" (ra'aytuni, "I saw myself") and "عَلِمْتُنِي" ('alimtuni, "I knew myself"). The meaning of ruya (رُؤْيَة, seeing) here is 'ilm (عِلْم, knowledge). Had it meant ibsar (إبْصار, sight with the eyes), it would be impermissible to combine the two pronouns with its verb.

﴿He thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ (اسْتَغْنى): this is the second object (al-maf'ul al-thani).

Indeed, to your Lord is the return (al-ruj'a).

This is a warning to the human being about the consequence of transgression (al-tughyan), expressed by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, from addressing a third person to addressing the second person directly). And "al-ruj'a" is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of "al-ruju'" (the return), i.e., your return is to your Lord, so He will requite you for your transgression.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ That is: Have you seen Abu Jahl forbidding Muhammad from prayer?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ That is: Have you seen Abu Jahl forbidding Muhammad from prayer?!
ﷻ "Have you seen, if he were upon guidance?" That is: if that forbidder were upon a sound course in what he forbids, namely the worship of Allah?!

Qur'an 96:12 — "Or he enjoins righteousness" (or he was one who enjoins what is good, and righteousness, in what he enjoins, [i.e., the worship of idols], as he believes).

Translation of the passage:

﴿Or enjoins righteousness﴾ — or he was one who enjoins good (al-ma'ruf), and righteousness (al-taqwa), in what he enjoins to of the worship of idols, as he believes it to be.

The Qur'anic verse ﴿Have you considered if he denies and turns away?﴾

Have you considered: if that forbidder was one who denies the truth and turns away from it?! As we say.

Qur'an quotations: ﴿Did he not know that Allah sees?﴾ — he is watching over his states, whether of guidance or misguidance, and will recompense him according to his condition. This is a warning (wa'id).

His saying "alladhi yanha" (the one who forbids), together with the conditional clause, are the two objects of "ara'ayta" (do you see). The answer of the condition is omitted (mahdhuf); its implied form is: "If he was upon guidance, or ordered piety, did he not know that Allah sees?" It was omitted because its mention in the answer of the second condition indicates it. This is like your saying: "If I honour you, will you honour me?" The second "ara'ayta" is repeated and superfluous, added for emphasis (li-l-tawkid).

"Kalla" (no! / indeed not), a rebuke to Abu Jahl for his forbidding the worship of Allah and his command to worship idols. Then He said: ﴿If he does not desist﴾ from what he is engaged in,

﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾, we will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire. "Al-safʿ" (seizing): grasping something and pulling it forcefully. Its spelling in the codex is with an alif (ناصية written with an alif after the ص, i.e., the word is written without the usual form), in accordance with the rule of pausal pronunciation (al-waqf). He dispensed with the definite article of previous mention (lam al-ʿahd) instead of a possessive pronoun, since it is known that it is the forelock of the one mentioned.

Surah 96, verse 16:

﴿Forelock﴾ is an appositive (badal) of "the forelock," because it is described as lying and sinning by His saying: ﴿lying, sinful﴾, through figurative attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), though both qualities really belong to its owner. In this there is a beauty and eloquence that are absent from your saying: "a lying, sinful forelock."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verse 17–18:

﴿Then let him call his council﴾ ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾. "Al-nadi" (the assembly): the gathering place where the people meet; and what is meant is the people of the assembly. It is related that "Abu Jahl passed by the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying, and said: Did I not forbid you? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke harshly to him, so he said: Do you threaten me, when I am the one with the greatest assembly in the valley?" ! Then the verses were revealed. And "al-zabaniyah" (the guards of Hell), linguistically: the police (al-shurat); the singular is "zibniyah," from "al-zabn," which is pushing, and what is meant is the angels of punishment. "And from him ﷺ: 'Had he called his council, the zabaniyah would have seized him openly.'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 96, verse 17–18:

﴿Then let him call his council﴾ ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾. "Al-nadi" (the assembly): the gathering place where the people meet; and what is meant is the people of the assembly. It is related that "Abu Jahl passed by the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying, and said: Did I not forbid you? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke harshly to him, so he said: Do you threaten me, when I am the one with the greatest assembly in the valley?" ! Then the verses were revealed. And "al-zabaniyah" (the guards of Hell), linguistically: the police (al-shurat); the singular is "zibniyah," from "al-zabn," which is pushing, and what is meant is the angels of punishment. "And from him ﷺ: 'Had he called his council, the zabaniyah would have seized him openly.'"

Kallā (ﷺ) — "Nay!" — is a rebuke directed at Abu Jahl.

﴿Do not obey him﴾, i.e., persist in what you are upon of disobedience to him, like His saying: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 8]. ﴿And prostrate﴾, and persist in your prostration, meaning the prayer.

﴿And draw near﴾, and seek nearness to your Lord through prostration, for the closest a servant comes to his Lord is when he prostrates. Such is the hadith.
